title: Insertion sort
summary: Sort like you sort playing cards in your hand.

cards.title: Cards in your hand
cards.body:
Pick up cards one at a time. Each new card slides left past bigger cards until it fits. The cards you are holding are **always sorted**.

That last sentence is the algorithm's **invariant**: a fact that stays true every step. Good programmers think in invariants.
Watch the `key`: it's the card being inserted. Bigger values shift right to make room.

cards.title: The code
cards.body: `while (j > 0 && a[j - 1] > key)` keeps shifting while the left neighbour is bigger. The order of the two conditions matters: `j > 0` is checked first, so `a[j - 1]` is never read at index -1.

cards.title: When insertion sort wins
cards.body:
Worst case it's O(n²), like bubble sort. But on **nearly sorted** data each card only moves a little, so it's close to **O(n)**.

That's why many `std::sort` implementations switch to insertion sort for tiny ranges: less overhead than the clever algorithms.

cards.question: Insertion sort is given `[1, 2, 3, 5, 4]`. Roughly how much work does it do?
cards.explain: Only the 4 is out of place and it moves one position. Every other card stops immediately. That's close to n steps.
